title: Chapter 45 – A Seam in the Quarry
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The quarry has been a trap for two nights, and Jian has not told anyone.

He built it alone, between funerals, in the hours when the hill was too tired to ask where a nineteen-year-old went with a coil of Hu's wire and a bag of iron pegs. It is not a clever trap. It is only a thing a boy might do who has looked at a map of ground and asked himself, over and over, if I were hurt, where would I lie?

The answer is the east wall.

It is the only place on the northern slope where the cut stone makes a shelf deep enough to hide in, and the only place where the old spoil heaps screen the wind. Four steps up, a low overhang. Below it, a drift of shattered slate. A hurt animal that wishes to be unfound will always choose the dry dark under a ledge, and a hurt Drip, bleeding, cut from her sister, will choose it twice.

He has strung six wires across the lower steps, at ankle height, tied to pegs. He has driven the pegs flat to the slate and covered them with grit. Along the face of the lowest step, in a hollow of the rock, he has laid a shallow pan of Hu's black slag, still faintly warm from the granary, and over it a skin of dead leaves. None of it will kill. All of it will tell him, by a flick on a thread, when someone walks where he does not wish her to.

Hu saw him, once. It was the second afternoon, at the granary door, with the wire on Jian's shoulder and the iron pegs in a sack.

"That is my wire," said the old man.

"Yes."

"It is good wire. It is for a ring. It is not for rabbits." Hu leaned on his bent rod and looked at the boy with his one clear eye, the other clouded and half shut. He had not touched wine in nine days. His hand shook a little on the rod. "I am going to ask you nothing. I have been asked nothing by better men, and it was a courtesy I did not deserve."

"Hu—"

"Use the black slag, not the gray. The gray cools too fast." He turned back into the dim of the granary. "And tell the little scaly one that the old man says thank you for the door."

Jian had not told him about the door. He had stood in the sunlight with the sack in his arms, and he had understood that Hu, who had spent forty years looking for seams in metal, had simply looked at a pangolin and a ring and a hill, and done the sum.

Now he stands in the middle of the quarry with the moon on his shoulder and Mother behind him, and the wires are quiet, and the wall is not.

Something is dragging itself along the stone.

* * *

Two, Pebble says. Small cold one. Bleeding. And another.

Another what?

A smell. Dog. A dog with no bark.

Shan, then. The tracker and his silent gray hound. The tracker has not fled. He has carried her out of the Narrows, Jian thinks, with something cold and exact settling in his stomach. He has been hauling a dying woman across the hills for three days, because Mu told him to bring back the sisters. The hound has followed her blood. And the hound has followed it to the only place in forty miles where the ground has already been opened.

He does not turn his head. He says, quietly, the words he said before. "Mother. The heap behind her."

Behind him, Qinghe is as still as a stone. The Veil has taken her so completely that he can hear only her breathing, and not even that. He thinks, with the part of his mind that never stops counting, that she is very good. He thinks she is the best he has ever seen. He is not at all surprised she is afraid.

She says, in the barest thread of sound: "What do I do?"

"If she runs, let her. If the dog runs, let it. If the man comes at me, call." He swallows. "I will not ask you to kill anyone."

"You did not ask," says Qinghe, "the last time."

It is not a rebuke. He hears that.

Then the stone speaks.

* * *

It is a tiny sound. A pebble, rolling. A scrape of cloth on slate. Then the breath of someone drawing air through her teeth, ragged and wet, and the soft slap of a hand on the rock.

Mei Ru comes out of the shadow of the overhang on her knees.

She is a ruin. Her rust-colored cloak is a rag. Her face is the color of tallow, with black circles round the eyes, and from her right sleeve hangs a stump of chain, torn off at the elbow. The skin of her arm below it is gone. She has bound it with strips of her own cloak. The binding is black. Under it, where the red line of the blood-link used to run from her wrist to her sister's, there is only a fraying, dead gray thread, drifting in the wind like a hair.

She looks up. She sees him. She smiles.

"There you are," says Mei Ru, softly. "Little boy."

"Mei Ru," he says.

"You know my name." She sounds pleased. "I wondered whether you would." She pushes herself to one knee. Her eyes, in the moonlight, are enormous. "I have been lying under that rock for four hours, listening to you walk. You step so lightly. I thought, that is a child who has been taught to be afraid." She tilts her head. "I do not think you are afraid of me."

"I am," says Jian. "But I have decided it is not important."

She laughs. It is a bubbling cracked sound, and a thread of blood runs from the corner of her mouth. "Oh, that's good. That is good. Do you know, my sister would have liked you. She liked people who said things. She was—" The laugh catches. "She was seventeen minutes older than me. Seventeen. I have never been without her for seventeen minutes."

"I'm sorry."

"No, you aren't." It is not unkind. "That is what is so interesting. You would do it again."

"Yes."

"Yes." Mei Ru nods slowly. "Well. I would, too."

Her right hand drops to her belt. In it is a short curved knife, black with old blood, and with a quick, tired, practiced movement she flicks it across her own palm and holds it up. Red wells.

"I should tell you what I am going to do," she says. "Because I think you would prefer to know. The sect has a small, ugly spell, called Blood Fox. It takes what is left of the blood in the body, and it burns it all at once, and it lets one run for the length of three breaths faster than the wind." She smiles, with terrible sweetness. "I will not live through it. I do not mind. I only want you to know that I will use it on you. I am going to take you with me, little boy. To the place the old men go. And I will have my sister there, and you will have an audience."

Jian does not move.

"Mother," he says, very quietly. "Now."

* * *

Several things happen at once.

Mei Ru's palm closes. The blood on it hisses into vapor, and a thin red line springs up her arm and over her shoulder, and her eyes go white. She is moving before he can finish the thought, in a blur, in a smear, across the slate in a straight line toward his throat.

From the shadow of the overhang, a gray streak launches itself, silent as smoke. It is the hound.

And the first wire, six inches from his left ankle, goes taut.

He has a hundredth of a breath. He spends it.

Pebble. Door.

Door! says Pebble, and there is a tearing. The air at the foot of the east wall rips like silk. A long hair-thin line of green light leaps up from the heap of broken stone and hangs there, a crack in the night a hand wide and as tall as a man.

Mei Ru, running full tilt, does not see it.

She sees only him, and so she goes through the seam.

* * *

The hound makes one sound. It is a short, high, human sort of yelp. It has gone four strides toward Jian, and it stops, slides on the slate, and looks back, and then, with a pure uncomplicated terror, it bolts the other way.

Shan comes out of the dark at a dead run. He has no weapon in his hands. He is a short broad man in a brown cloak, with a flattened nose and a face like a closed door, and at this moment the face is open. It is naked with horror.

"Girl!" he shouts. "Ru! No!"

Jian is facing the wrong way. He has pivoted to throw, with the first needle already humming on its thread, and the sister is not there. There is a place in the air where she was, a hole in the world, and a long thin scream, coming from a great distance.

It took her. The seam took her.

Not took, Pebble whispers. Opened. She ran into the cold place. The cold place does not like being run into.

The green gap is shuddering. It is narrowing. He sees its edges tremble, as if at the end of a long held breath.

"She's in the wall," says Shan. His voice is a ragged whisper. "In the wall." He staggers to a stop three paces from Jian, with his empty hands out in front of him, and looks at the boy and the needle, and the gap. His eyes are wet. "What is that? What have you done?"

"I haven't done anything."

"Liar." But there is no heat in it. "Liar. Liar. She was nineteen when I took her in. I taught her to read tracks." He swallows. "She called me uncle."

Jian lets the needle drift. He says, as gently as he knows how: "Go home, Shan."

"Mu will have my skin."

"Then do not go to Mu."

The man stares at him. For a moment something in the broken-nosed face looks almost like hope. Then the hound whines, somewhere in the dark, and Shan's mouth twists.

"He will find you," he says. "You and the beast. He has lilies in his garden that are older than your grandfather. He is not a man who forgets." He steps back. "You are not a boy. I understand that now. I understand that it was always a trick."

"Go."

Shan does not move. He looks at the place where the seam is closing, and at the boy, and at his own empty hands. "She was the last," he says, hoarsely. "Of the Drips Mu raised. Her and the sister. The rest are men he bought." He shakes his head. "He will not forgive it. Not for the girls. For the drum. A drum like that takes thirty years to make."

"Then tell him it was a hard road."

"I will tell him nothing." The tracker's broken-nosed face works. "I will tell him the truth, that the boy who counts was not a boy, and that the hill is not a hill. And I will ask for my release. And he will give it, because I have never lied to him once in forty years, and he is a man who values a clean tool." A thin bitter smile. "It is the only reason I am still alive."

He goes. He goes in a stumbling run, up the slope, away from the quarry, with the hound a gray streak ahead of him in the dark. The sound of his boots fades. In a moment there is only the wind.

The seam is closing.

* * *

Jian stands in front of it with a thread of Qi trailing from his fingertips.

He can feel the weight of the decision in every muscle of his back. He is a youth of nineteen. There is a dying woman on the other side of a hole in the night, who meant to kill him and has, by an accident of speed and spite, gone through a door that did not open for her. He has a cracked rib. He has five needles left in his roll. His Qi reserve is low, and falling.

He should stay. Every sentence in him says: stay. A seam is not a door. A seam is a thing that Hu's old master said could eat a man whole. He has no idea what it leads to.

But she is alive, he thinks. She might still be alive. And she will come back, if she can, and she will tell Mu what she saw.

And what I have not told anyone, says the colder, quieter part of him, is that I want to know.

He does not say it aloud. He has learned not to. But he feels it with the whole of his small cold body, a strange hot hook of wanting, set in his chest like a fishhook. He has been standing at the edge of the Hill of Green Pine for ten years, with his hands in his sleeves, and today for the first time in his life the edge has opened.

```
[ARK-7 — SCAN]

Origin: Hill of Green Pine, depth ~600 m (estimate low confidence).
Qi density at aperture: 340% of local baseline.
Structure: Non-mineral. Non-geometric. Shows self-repair.
Level 2 Scan: INSUFFICIENT AUTHORITY.

Four breaths.

"Jian," says Mother, behind him. It is quite calm. It is the calm of a woman holding an iron rail with both hands. "Do not."

"I know."

"Do not go in."

"I know, Mother." He turns his head. She has dropped the Veil. She is standing five paces off, with her hood fallen back and her knife in one hand and the moon making a silver ring of her hair. He has never seen her so afraid. "I am going to try not to. But I think the seam is going to close on its own, and I think that when it does, Mei Ru will be in there with whatever is in there, and I think that is the only thing I have ever done that I cannot undo."

She says nothing.

"I want to look," he says, low. "Only look. I will come back."

"You cannot promise that."

"No."

She takes a step toward him. Her hand comes out. And in the green light, at the edge of the closing seam, something small and pale detaches itself from his collar and drops to the gravel.

Pebble.

Door, says Pebble. She is looking at the gap. Her round black eyes are wide and shining. I know this door.

"Pebble—"

I know it. It is a big place. It is a good place. It is a place with water. It smells of mother. A tremble runs through her whole small body. I did not know until now. I am sorry. I was afraid to say.

"What place?"

The place I was born, says Pebble.

* * *

Mother's hand closes on his sleeve.

He feels it. A strong, cool, narrow hand, with callus at the base of each finger from twenty years of herbs and blades. For a moment he thinks she will pull him back.

"If you are not out by dawn," says Qinghe, very low, "I will come in after you. I do not care what is there."

"Yes."

"And you will tell me everything. When you come out. Everything." Her grip tightens. "Not as a mother asks. As a clan asks."

"Yes."

"Then go."

She lets go.

He steps forward. The seam is a vertical line of green fire, a thread's width, taller than he is, humming faintly like a struck bell. It smells of earth, wet and black and sweet. It smells of tomato leaves and crushed mint and cold stone and something very old, the memory of a place where things grew before there were any people to name them.

Pebble runs up his sleeve. He feels her tiny claws catch in the cloth, and settle under his collar.

Together, she says.

"Together."

He puts out his hand.

The seam does not resist. It parts. It opens in front of him like the lips of a long green mouth, and the cold of it goes up his arm, and through his chest, and into his head. For one instant every wire in the quarry, every peg, every pan of slag, every cracked wall and long shadow, becomes sharp and clear and infinitely distant. For one instant he sees himself from outside: a small boy in a gray robe, hand out, at the foot of a wall, in the moonlight, with a woman behind him whose face is wet.

Then the green swallows it all, and he falls.

In the last half-second he thinks of Hu's drawing paper, and the map in his own hand, and the three words he wrote on it. He thinks of Mao, who counted breaths. He thinks, absurdly, of the schoolmaster's voice reading out the rules of the Register: Entry is voluntary. Exit is at the discretion of the clan. He has never been so entirely outside any rule.

He does not stop. He has not stopped once, he realizes, since the morning he opened his eyes in a dead boy's body and learned the shape of the world by the edges. He is not sure whether that is courage, or only a very long habit.

* * *

It is not a long fall. Perhaps a heartbeat.

He lands on his hands and knees on something soft. It gives, springs, bounces a little under his weight. Moss. Deep, wet, cold moss, thick as a mattress. It smells like the inside of a forest after rain.

The dark is not dark. A thin pearly light is coming from everywhere, from the air, from the ground, from the slow drift of a million tiny motes that hang like dust in a sunbeam, and all of them are faintly, tenderly green. Above him is not a sky. It is a ceiling, a huge, low, arched, glowing ceiling of pale stone, far higher than any hall, and across it run veins of silver, like a map of rivers.

He pushes himself to his feet. His rib sings. His breath comes out in a white cloud.

Before him, vanishing into the green haze in every direction, stretch row upon row of tall dark plants. They grow in beds of black earth, between curving walls of pale stone, and each bed is bordered by a ring of tiny white pebbles. He knows the pattern. He has seen it before, in a dream, a month ago, when Pebble first slept against his heart.

An orchard with no sky.

Home, whispers Pebble, in a voice so small that he thinks he has imagined it. Home. Home. Home.

He breathes in, and nearly staggers.

The air is thick. It does not feel thick. It feels like nothing, like breath, like a spring morning. But the Qi in it presses on his channels like warm water pressing on a sponge, and every pore he owns opens at once. His reserve, which was nearly empty in the quarry, fills in the space of ten breaths. His rib stops aching. For the first time in two months his head is clear.

This is what the hill was, once, he thinks. Before the vein faded. Before the Founder died.

```

Not recommended. He reads the last line twice. The interface has never before offered an opinion, only a cost. It is like being told by a well-meaning friend that the soup is probably hot.

He takes one slow step, and then another, along the nearest bed. The plants are taller than he is. Their leaves are broad and dark, with a faint silver sheen, and from the base of each stem a pale tendril winds into the soil like a vein. Near the path, a small red fruit hangs from a branch no thicker than a thread. It glows, very slightly, from inside.

Do not eat, says Pebble sharply. Do not eat. Not yet. Not here.

"I wasn't going to."

You were thinking about it.

He was. He folds his hands behind his back.

The beds run in straight lines to the limit of the glow, and beyond it, in the haze, other shapes loom, a long low terrace, a thin arch like a bridge, a faint round gleam that might be water. There are no footprints in the moss. No tools. No door. Only the green hush, and the slow drift of light, and the feeling, every second more certain, of being watched by something that is not unfriendly, and not at all sleepy.

And ten paces off, face-down in the moss with her hands flung out in front of her, a woman in a torn rust-colored cloak is lying very still.

He goes to her. He kneels. He puts two fingers against the cold side of her throat, and waits.

Nothing. Then, slowly, very faintly, a flutter.

"Oh," says Jian softly. "You're not dead."

He sits back on his heels and looks at her.

She meant to take me with her. She would do it again. The thought is plain and cold. The Veil is gone from him; the needle roll is warm against his chest. Five needles. One thread through the base of the skull, and no one on this earth would ever know. It would be, he thinks, the sensible thing.

He does not move.

She is seventeen minutes younger than a dead woman, he thinks. She called him little boy and meant it kindly. He does not know why that is the thing that stops him. He has killed four people in two months, and each time he has been able to say because. He cannot find a because here. She is a hurt animal in a strange room.

Pebble is on the moss beside her, sniffing at the torn rust cloak with her small wet nose. She smells of blood, she reports. Old blood. Not bad. Just tired.

"Tired," says Jian.

All of them are tired, says Pebble, as if it were a simple fact of nature.

He unties the roll at his belt. Hu pressed three pills into his hand at the funeral without a word, from the bottles Tally carried, and he has kept them without knowing why. Blood Seal, Level One, medium grade. Not for internal use, the slip said. Stops bleeding from a non-vital wound within five breaths.

He crushes one between his fingers and sprinkles the dust over the black binding on her stump of an arm. It hisses. The dark stain stops spreading. After a moment, a faint, grudging color comes back to her lip.

That is a bad decision, the cold part of him observes. Possibly the worst you have made.

Probably, he agrees.

Behind him, with no sound at all, the green seam in the air folds shut.
